content: In 2007, ConAgra Foods initiated a recall of its Banquet and generic brand chicken and turkey pot pies after 152 cases of salmonella poisoning were reported across 31 states, with 20 individuals requiring hospitalization. By October 12, the recall was expanded to include all varieties of frozen pot pies sold under multiple brand names, such as Banquet, Albertson’s, Food Lion, and others. The affected products were 7-ounce single-serving packages marked with P-9 or Est 1059. In 2007, the Topps Meat Company in New Jersey was responsible for an E. coli O157:H7 outbreak linked to ground beef, resulting in the second-largest beef recall in U.S. history. In 2007, Metz Fresh recalled 8,000 cartons of fresh spinach due to salmonella contamination, though no illnesses were reported. In 2007, Castleberry Foods recalled over 25 brands of canned chili sauce and other products due to botulism contamination. The affected products had best by dates ranging from April 30, 2009, to May 22, 2009. Botulism in commercially canned products is extremely rare, with the last U.S. case dating back to the 1970s. Most botulism cases in the U.S. are linked to home-canned foods. In 2007, an outbreak of salmonella linked to Peter Pan and Great Value peanut butter affected 425 individuals across 44 states. This was the first documented salmonella outbreak associated with peanut butter in U.S. history. In 2006, an E. coli O157:H7 outbreak linked to Taco Bell sickened 39 people in New Jersey and Long Island. Initially, green onions were suspected, but later investigations pointed to contaminated lettuce. Taco Bell removed green onions from its menu, leading to a public relations issue and a pending lawsuit. In 2006, an E. coli O157:H7 outbreak associated with bagged spinach from Natural Selection Foods resulted in 3 deaths and 198 illnesses across 25 U.S. states, as well as 1 case in Ontario, Canada. In 2003, a hepatitis A outbreak in Pennsylvania was linked to green onions. In 2002, ConAgra recalled over 19 million pounds of ground beef due to E. coli O157:H7 contamination. The outbreak sickened 19 people across six states, making it the third-largest beef recall in U.S. history. In 2002, Pilgrim’s Pride recalled over 27 million pounds of processed chicken due to listeria contamination. The outbreak caused 7 deaths, 46 illnesses, and 3 miscarriages, marking the largest poultry recall in U.S. history. In 2001, salmonella contamination in unpasteurized orange juice from Sun Orchard in Arizona was traced to ice used to cool imported orange juice from Mexico. In 2000, salmonella in bean sprouts from Pacific Coast Sprout Farms caused an outbreak from Oregon to Massachusetts. At least 67 people became ill, and 17 were hospitalized. The contamination was linked to dry seeds imported from China and Australia. In 1997, a hepatitis A outbreak was linked to frozen strawberries from Andrew & Williamson Sales Co. The strawberries, grown in Baja California, Mexico, were served in school lunches, potentially exposing thousands of students across six states. Over 2.6 million pounds of strawberries were recalled. In 1997, Hudson Foods Company recalled over 25 million pounds of ground beef due to E. coli O157:H7 contamination. The outbreak was linked to a plant in Nebraska, and Burger King was the largest client affected. In 1996, an E. coli O157:H7 outbreak was linked to unpasteurized apple juice from Odwalla. In 1994, salmonella contamination in ice cream from Schwan’s Sales Enterprises sickened over 3,000 people across 41 states. The contamination occurred when raw, unpasteurized eggs were transported in a tanker truck that later carried pasteurized ice cream mix. In 1993, an E. coli O157:H7 outbreak linked to undercooked hamburgers from Jack in the Box resulted in 4 deaths and hundreds of illnesses in the Seattle area and the Pacific Northwest. In 1992, botulism was reported in New Jersey after four members of a family consumed contaminated whitefish. In 1985, listeria contamination in Mexican-style soft cheese in Southern California caused 47 deaths, including 19 stillbirths and 10 infant deaths, making it the deadliest foodborne outbreak in recent U.S. history. In 1985, salmonella in milk from a Chicago-area dairy caused over 16,000 confirmed cases of food poisoning across six Midwest states, with two confirmed deaths and potentially 12 more related fatalities. In 1985, botulism outbreaks occurred at two White Spot restaurants in Vancouver, British Columbia, due to chopped garlic stored in soybean oil. In 1983, a botulism outbreak in Peoria, Illinois, was linked to sautéed onions served on patty melt sandwiches at a restaurant. The outbreak hospitalized 28 people, with 12 requiring ventilatory support and 1 death reported. In 1974, salmonella in unpasteurized apple cider caused 200 illnesses in New Jersey. In 1971, botulism in vichyssoise soup manufactured by Bon Vivant, Inc., led to a recall of 6,444 cans. The FDA later expanded the recall to include all Bon Vivant products due to concerns about the company’s processing practices. The incident destroyed public confidence in the brand, leading to the company’s bankruptcy.
